title: Count Words With a String Stream
statement:
`std::cin >> someString` already knows how to skip whitespace and stop at
the next run of it -- that is exactly what "split on whitespace" means,
and `std::istringstream` gives you the same operator over a string you
already have in memory instead of over actual standard input.

## Your function

```
int CountWords(const std::string& text);
```

Return how many whitespace-separated words `text` contains. Words may be
separated by any run of spaces or tabs, of any length; leading and
trailing whitespace do not count as words. `text` may be empty.

## Watch out

- **Runs of whitespace, not single spaces, separate words.** `"a   b"`
  (three spaces) has exactly two words, the same as `"a b"` -- counting
  every space character, or every gap between characters, overcounts runs
  of more than one.
- **Leading and trailing whitespace contribute no extra words.**
  `"  hello  "` has one word, not three; splitting naively on a single
  space character and counting the resulting pieces (including empty ones
  at the ends) gets this wrong.
- **An `std::istringstream` fed by `>>` in a `while` loop does the whole
  job correctly on its own** -- it already treats a run of whitespace as
  one separator and produces nothing for leading or trailing whitespace,
  which is exactly the specification above, not a coincidence.

tests.name: an empty line has no words
runs of multiple spaces between words
tests.description: Three separators, each more than one space wide -- still three words, not more.

tests.name: leading and trailing whitespace do not add words
a line that is whitespace only has no words
